zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent scan reading: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Its spellings are not treated as authority for the printed glyphs.

lines.note: Continues an entry from the preceding page: the Japanese refers to the mourning interval for the sovereign. The scan reads ſaſu, “denotes/refers to,” not OCR ſatu; the unmarked spelling chuin is retained.

runs.text: em que morreo o Rey, por eſtar tudo ẽ treuas.

lines.note: Completes the Portuguese explanation as the period following the king’s death, when everything is in darkness. The abbreviation ẽ is preserved rather than expanded to em.
Ryōba is here two horses, explicitly paraphrased as ni hiki no uma. Nifiqino preserves the historical h-row spelling and the attached particle.
Ryōbai denotes a good intermediary or matchmaker; yoi nakadachi and bom terceiro agree in identifying the mediating person.
Ryōbō, alternatively ryōhō, means both sides. The synonym reads Futatçuno cata; its second t is visible, correcting OCR Furatçuno.
As partes completes Ambas from the preceding row: both parties or sides, not an independent definition.
Ryōboku is good timber or a good tree. The closely set Japanese Yoqiqi is retained, and the Portuguese specifies wood suitable for building below.
Madeira completes pao pera madeira, clarifying the useful-timber sense of the preceding entry.

runs.text: Proprias terras, ou renda, ou dentro

lines.note: Ryōbun concerns one’s own domain, income, or being within that domain; the last construction continues onto the next row.
Completes dentro das terras dalguem, within someone’s lands. The contraction dalguem remains as printed.
Ryōka is glossed as two houses or families. The damaged headword retains a visible i between R and the marked o; the crop supports Riǒca rather than OCR Rǒca.

Riôca has the alternative Riôga and the paraphrase Teiuǒno norimono, the sovereign’s conveyance. Both alternative headwords have roof-shaped accents in the enlargement; Riôga corrects the draft Ruôga. The Portuguese An- continues with das on the next line.
Das completes An-das, the royal palanquin or litter named on the preceding row. Keep the physical word division.
Ryōchi denotes an estate, lands, or income. Erdade is the printed Portuguese form and is not modernized to herdade.
Ryōchū, alternatively ryōnai, means within one’s domain. The initial is R rather than OCR B, and the final u bears a caron.
Renda que hum tem completes the territorial or revenue-holding definition. It does not begin a new entry.
Ryōko is two tigers, futatsu no tora. Vide introduces a cross-reference whose Japanese headword appears on the following row.

Reǒco is the Japanese cross-reference introduced by Vide on the preceding row. The downward-pointing vowel mark supports a caron rather than the draft’s grave. The compact type is not entirely distinct; the aligned draft’s italic classification is retained and the word is flagged for typeface review.

runs.text: Riocuchicu. Midorino taqe. i, Auoi ta-

lines.note: Ryokuchiku means green bamboo, given by midori no take and aoi take. The last word is physically divided ta-/qe.
Qe completes take; the Portuguese says green bamboos. S. is the upright written-register label rather than part of the italic gloss.
Ryokuhatsu denotes beautiful hair of the head. Preserve the checked-coda spelling fat and the historical Portuguese fermoſos.
Dos completes lin-dos, reinforcing the description of fine hair. The following upright S. marks written usage.
Ryokuin is green or leafy shade, midori no kage. The Portuguese explains cool shade, retaining the abbreviation Sõbra.
The shade is cast by many trees while they are green. This completes the preceding gloss, including printed eſtam rather than a modernized ending.

runs.text: Riocuju. Midorino vyeqi. i, Auoqi qi.

lines.note: Ryokuju is a green tree, explained by midori no uyeki and aoki ki. Ar- begins the Portuguese noun on the next row.
Uore completes Ar-uore, followed by verde and freſca. The scan supports verde, not OCR veide, and the final S. is upright.
Ryokura is green ivy, midori no tsuta. Portuguese Era is the printed historical form; do not insert a modern initial h. S. marks written use.

runs.text: Riocusǒ. Midorino cuſa. i, Auoi cuſa.

lines.note: Ryokusō means green grass. The downward-pointing mark supports Riocusǒ rather than OCR Riocusô; midori no kusa and aoi kusa provide matching synonyms.
Verde completes Erua verde, green grass. The upright S. remains separate from the italic explanation.
Ryokusui denotes green water. The final i of Riocuſui and the abbreviation mark in q̃ are visible; both were omitted by OCR.

runs.text: ſer em muita quãtidade parece verde.

lines.note: The water appears green because of its great quantity. The verb is parece, not parete; quãtidade retains its printed abbreviation, and S. is a usage label.

runs.text: Riocutai. Midorino coqe. i, Auoi coqe.

lines.note: Ryokutai is green moss, explained by midori no koke and aoi koke. Both occurrences of coqe use the ordinary historical k-series spelling.
Muſgo verde supplies the Portuguese gloss “green moss.” The final S. is the upright written-register marker.
Ryōdan is glossed as two things rather than silently reinterpreted from a possible modern compound. S. is printed in upright type.
Ryōdo is twice, futatabi. The conspicuous space in Riǒ do is retained as printed; it does not create a separate lexical item in the interpretation.
Ryōhen is two sorts or aspects of things, explained by futasama no koto. The Portuguese list of kinds and forms continues below.
Completes the two sorts or forms of things in the preceding entry. Feições is retained with its printed cedilla and tilde.
Ryōhō is both sides, directly matching Ambas as partes. This is a separate entry despite its earlier appearance as an alternative under Riǒbǒ.

The gloss identifies a cool wind, suzushii kaze. The headword is abraded; Riofù retains the provisional unmarked o and grave-marked u rather than supplying the marks expected from the lexical reading ryōfū.
Ryōfu means two husbands. The scan restores initial R and f in place of OCR iǒru; Vt introduces the maxim that follows.
Teijo ryōfu ni mamiezu says that a chaste woman does not unite with two husbands. The Portuguese translation begins with A molher caſ-, divided across the row boundary.

runs.text: ta e conſtante não ſe ajunta com dous maridos.

lines.note: Ta completes caſta; the translation adds steadfastness and says she does not join with two husbands. The historical moral claim is transcribed without extending it beyond the source.

runs.text: Dous terminos. Item, Duas couſas, ou

lines.note: Ryōgai is glossed as two terms or limits, and then as two things or persons. The explanation continues into the mandala example below.
Ryōgai no mandara is followed by the source’s explanation in terms of a male and female Fotoque. Fotoque occurs within the Portuguese gloss and is flagged for whole-word typeface review.

Completes the source’s paired male/female explanation. Fotoque is a Japanese term embedded in Portuguese, retained in the aligned draft’s italic setting after reinspection; the final upright S. marks written usage.
Ryōgan denotes both eyes, futatsu no manako. The abbreviation mark over final a is visible, so Riǒgã is retained rather than OCR Riǒga; the NINJAL index corroborates the lexical identification.
Ryōjin is two armies, expressed by futatsu no jin. The Portuguese alternative “both armies” continues below.
Completes the preceding definition as both armies. The damaged sequence is osexercitos rather than OCR otexercitos; its close printed spacing is retained.

Ryōjō is glossed as two things or two chapters/sections. The scan supports Riǒgiô rather than OCR Bǒgiô. Capitulos is the chosen Portuguese reading rather than capiuros, although abrasion leaves its middle letters somewhat uncertain.
Ryōjū is explained by futakasane, two layers or doublings. The Portuguese du- begins duas on the following row.
As completes du-as and defines two doubled things. This is a physical continuation of the layering entry.
Ryōgoku is two countries or kingdoms, explicitly equated with nikakoku. Preserve the historical Nicacocu spelling.
Ryōge chigai suru illustrates differing in understanding. The divided Portuguese Diſcre- begins the corresponding verb.

runs.text: par, ou deſencõtrarenſe dous em entender al-

lines.note: Par completes Diſcre-par; the alternative describes two people failing to agree in their understanding of something. The printed deſencõtrarenſe is retained without modernizing its ending.
Gũa completes al-gũa, finishing “some thing” in the preceding disagreement gloss. The abbreviation tilde remains over u.
The second Ryōgue entry uses satori toku, understanding or penetrating a teaching. The Portuguese noun is entendimento, not OCR entendiments.

runs.text: ou penetrar bem as couſas do Buppô.

lines.note: Completes the gloss as understanding the matters of Buddhist teaching. Buppô is a Japanese term within the Portuguese explanation, retained in italic and flagged for whole-word typeface review; the circumflex is visible, and penetrar replaces OCR oenetrar.
Ryōget first denotes a fine, clear moon, yo(k)i tsuki. The word’s bare final t is retained, and fermo- continues below.

runs.text: ſa. Item, Duas lũas, ou dous meſes de Iapão.

lines.note: Sa completes fermoſa; a second sense is two moons or two Japanese months. The two senses remain under this one printed headword.
Ryōgi is two things, futatsu no koto. The damaged initial is R, not the OCR’s B.

runs.text: Riǒgun. Futatçuno icuſa. i, Futatçuno gin.

lines.note: Ryōgun is paraphrased as two armies, futatsu no ikusa and futatsu no jin. The last word is gin with final n, correcting OCR gir.
Dous exercitos completes the two-armies definition. It is not part of the following territorial sense of the same headword.

runs.text: Duas partes, ou comarcas do reino.

lines.note: The second Ryōgun denotes two districts or divisions of a kingdom. Its initial R is distinguishable from OCR B.
Ryō-i is a good physician. The hyphen belongs within the printed headword and is not a physical-line continuation mark.
Ryōzetsu is literally two tongues, shita futatsu; the Portuguese uses “two mouths.” The example’s Riǒ- is divided from jetna below.

runs.text: Peßoa que fala por duas bo-

lines.note: Jetna mono completes the phrase for a double-tongued person. The Portuguese translation continues bo-/cas across the physical row boundary.

runs.text: cas, ou que varia no que diz.

lines.note: Cas completes bocas, followed by varying what one says. The gloss explains inconsistency or duplicity of speech, not two physical mouths.
Ryōji denotes a good warrior, yo(k)i tsuwamono. The Portuguese is ſoldado, with long s rather than f; upright S. precedes the italic example marker.
Meikun wa ryōji wo sutsuru koto nashi says that a good lord does not cast aside a good warrior. The Portuguese translation begins with capital O.

runs.text: bom ſenhor não deita fora o bõ caualeiro.

lines.note: Completes the good-lord maxim. Xix. is the upright source label; bõ is retained as the printed abbreviation in the description of the warrior.
Ryōjō means consent, explained by Vqegǒ. The example repeats the headword across Riǒ-/jǒ; the missing i in OCR Rǒ- is restored from the scan.
Jǒ ſuru completes the example “to consent.” This short Japanese continuation remains its own physical row.

Ryōju is a good tree, yo(k)i ki. The example begins Riǒjuuo, with initial R rather than OCR F; its injunction continues on the next row. The aligned draft’s Vt. punctuation is retained after reinspection.
Ki(ru) koto nakare is a prohibition on cutting the good tree. The Portuguese translation divides ar-uore across this boundary.
Uore completes the Portuguese word for tree. The following upright S. marks written usage.

runs.text: Senhor, ou dono dalgũa rẽda, ou terras.

lines.note: The second Ryōju is the lord or owner of an income or lands. The abbreviation in rẽda and the u-carried tilde in dalgũa remain unexpanded.
Ryōmen means two faces; Futatçuno cauo supplies the corresponding Japanese phrase. The first u is visible, correcting OCR Fotatçuno.
A further sense is both sides. The example begins Riǒmen-, completed as a writing-related compound on the next row.

runs.text: O eſcreuer dambas as partes do papel.

lines.note: Gaqi completes ryōmengaki, writing on both sides of the paper. The entry ends with a period after papel, not the OCR’s spurious hyphen.
Ryōmengaqi ſuru refers back to the same two-sided writing. The example’s differing circumflex-like mark is retained as Riômengaqi rather than regularized to the headword.

runs.text: Dentro da erdade, terras, ou renda

lines.note: Ryōnai is within an estate, lands, or income-holding. The Portuguese list reads terras with lowercase t, not OCR Ierras.
Dalguem completes the preceding possessive expression, describing someone’s domain. It remains a separate physical continuation.
Ryōni is both ears, futatsu no mimi. The bilateral sense is explicit in the Portuguese Ambas as orelhas.
Ryōnichi means two days. This brief complete entry is distinct from the following word for two people.
Ryōnin means two people, futari no hito. Homẽs retains the printed nasal abbreviation.

runs.text: Entender, ou perceber com o entendi-

lines.note: Ryōnō is to understand or perceive intellectually. The Portuguese word divides entendi-/mento; OCR’s final s and period are not supported.
Mento completes entendimento. Ryōnō shita is then translated as “I understood” or “I perceived.”

runs.text: Official nobre, q̃ da parte dos Cũgues ſe

lines.note: Ryōke is described as a noble official appointed on behalf of the court nobles. Cũgues is a Japanese-derived designation within the Portuguese description and is flagged for typeface review.

runs.text: punha antiguamẽte pera gouernar as rẽdas dos

lines.note: The official was formerly installed to administer the court nobles’ revenues. Antiguamẽte and rẽdas preserve the source’s abbreviations.

runs.text: Cũgues q̃ eſtauão de miſtura cõ as de algũ ſenhor

lines.note: The revenues concerned were intermingled with those of a military lord. The repeated Cũgues remains within the Portuguese explanation, not a new headword.

runs.text: ſoldado: o outro cõpanheiro da parte dos ſoldados

lines.note: The colon distinguishes the military lord from the corresponding representative appointed by the warrior side. The scan restores ſoldado: o outro and ſoldados where OCR garbled the words.

The counterpart was called Gitô, identifying the jitō office. Enlargement clearly shows capital G, i, t and circumflex o, replacing OCR Chtô; the Japanese term is upright within the Portuguese sentence.

Ryōkyaku denotes both legs, futatsu no hagi. The second noun is fagui, with a looped g, in the source’s historical spelling; the synonym reads Futatçuno rather than OCR Futatçono. Per- continues as nas on the next row.
Nas completes per-nas; pees adds feet as the alternative Portuguese gloss. The scan supports pees, not OCR pres.
Ryōkin no ōgi is a fan gilded on both sides, with Abano beginning a gloss continued on the next page. The headword is Riǒqin, not Reiǒqin, and Abano replaces OCR Abamo.
